content: Marijuana has demonstrated anti-epileptic effects in animal studies. However, its effectiveness in treating epilepsy in human patients remains unknown. Despite this uncertainty, some states in the United States have explicitly approved the use of marijuana for epilepsy treatment. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of cannabinoids, either as a standalone treatment or as an add-on therapy, for individuals with epilepsy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, ISI Web of Knowledge, CINAHL, and ClinicalTrials.gov, all as of September 9, 2013. Additionally, studies known to the authors but not identified in the database searches, as well as references from identified studies, were included. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), regardless of whether they were blinded. Two independent authors selected the trials for inclusion and extracted the relevant data. The primary outcome of interest was seizure freedom for a duration of one year or more, or three times the longest interseizure interval. Secondary outcomes included the responder rate at six months or more, objective quality of life measures, and adverse events. The review identified four randomized trial reports involving a total of 48 patients. In all these studies, cannabidiol (CBD) was used as the treatment agent. One of the reports was presented as an abstract, and another was a letter to the editor. In all studies, patients continued their use of anti-epileptic drugs alongside cannabidiol. None of the reports provided details about the randomization process, nor did they investigate whether the control and treatment groups were comparable. The quality of all four reports was deemed low. These studies only addressed the secondary outcome of adverse effects, and none of the patients in the treatment groups experienced any adverse effects. The authors concluded that no reliable conclusions can currently be drawn regarding the efficacy of cannabinoids as a treatment for epilepsy. Cannabidiol doses of 200 to 300 mg per day were safely administered to small numbers of patients, typically for short durations. However, the safety of long-term cannabidiol treatment cannot be reliably assessed based on the available data.
